title: Marriage data reveals traditional nuclear families are disappearing across US — with a rate of just 13% in one major city | Institute for Family Studies
gist: A New York Post write-up (teaser only) of an IFS report on 'marriage deserts': in some neighborhoods of Cleveland, Washington DC, Milwaukee and Detroit fewer than a quarter of households with children are headed by married couples, contrasted with suburban 'married-family gardens'. The headline cites 13% in one major city, but the excerpt itself does not give the city.

insights.claim: An IFS report on 'marriage deserts' finds that in certain neighborhoods of Cleveland, Washington DC, Milwaukee and Detroit fewer than a quarter of households with children are headed by married couples.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Family structure is geographically polarized; neighborhood-level household composition is a lens on local social capital and demand for family-oriented services.

insights.claim: Marriage deserts in urban neighborhoods contrast with suburban-centric 'married-family gardens', showing a spatial divide in where the married-parent household persists.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Suggests married-family households cluster in suburbs, a demographic backdrop for suburban housing and family-oriented consumption versus urban cores.
insights.locator: emphasized a divide between these deserts and suburban-centric “married-family gardens.”

insights.claim: The nuclear family structure that once dominated American households is disappearing across the country, particularly in parts of major cities, according to the IFS report.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Secular decline of the married-parent household shapes long-run household formation, fertility and public-service demand.
insights.locator: The nuclear family structure that once dominated American households is disappearing
